name: Aluminum chloride hexahydrate (Drysol)

lead: Prescription-strength aluminium chloride keeps underarms, and sometimes hands and feet, dry and clothes free of sweat marks.

It is an astringent salt that reduces sweat output at the skin, at higher concentrations than ordinary antiperspirants, which typically use aluminium chlorohydrate. Dermatology sources and guidelines describe topical antiperspirants as first-line for hyperhidrosis, and a few small registered studies compare it with other treatments.

paras: It is applied as a liquid to dry skin, commonly at night. Improvement is described as taking several days, after which use is often spaced out.

Skin irritation is the common effect. The label restricts sale and use to licensed practitioners. Aluminium exposure has been studied in other contexts, including a 2005 review on antiperspirants and breast cancer.

angle.text: Prescription-strength aluminium chloride is used on underarms, and sometimes hands and feet, to keep skin dry and clothes free of sweat marks. It plugs and calms sweat output at the skin, so the result is visible in use. Dermatology sources describe it as a first-line treatment for hyperhidrosis.

lead: Aluminium chloride hexahydrate is the active ingredient in prescription-strength antiperspirants such as Drysol, used to reduce excessive sweating (hyperhidrosis) of the underarms, palms and feet. For appearance, the payoff is a drier look: fewer visible sweat marks on shirts, less clamminess in handshakes and less sweat-related odour and clothing staining. Dermatology reviews describe antiperspirants as the first-line therapy for primary focal hyperhidrosis, with aluminium salts as the mainstay [1][2].

Aluminium salts work by reacting with sweat in the duct of the eccrine gland and forming a plug that blocks sweat from reaching the skin surface [2][3]. Prescription products use aluminium chloride hexahydrate in an alcohol base at higher concentrations than over-the-counter antiperspirants, which typically use aluminium chlorohydrate [4][5]. Skin irritation is the most commonly reported side effect, and the US label carries the statement that sale and use are restricted to a physician or licensed practitioner [6].

Research includes small controlled trials dating from the 1970s and 1990s and more recent comparisons with oral drugs and botulinum toxin [7][8][9]. Aluminium in antiperspirants has also been the subject of public concern about breast cancer and Alzheimer's disease, which cancer and toxicology bodies have reviewed [10][3].
infobox: Label restricts sale and use to a physician or licensed practitioner [6]

paras: People with heavy underarm, hand or foot sweating use prescription aluminium chloride to keep clothes dry, avoid visible sweat patches and reduce odour. Clinicians note that sweating beyond what the body needs for temperature control can affect quality of life and social confidence [1]. Men on the T Nation forum have traded tips on prescription and behind-the-counter aluminium chloride products for this purpose, naming Drysol as a leading form [11].

Because sweat marks and wet palms are noticeable in social and professional settings, dry skin is part of grooming for people affected by hyperhidrosis, alongside clothing choices and fabric selection.

Primary focal hyperhidrosis affects about 3 percent of the US population, according to a dermatology clinics review, and more than half of those affected have underarm involvement [2]. Reference works describe topical antiperspirants as the first step before oral drugs, injections, devices or surgery [1]. A review of laser treatment calls topical aluminium chloride hexahydrate at 10 to 20 percent the current standard of care [5].

Reference works say effects take roughly three to five days to appear and that it works especially well on the underarms. A palmoplantar hyperhidrosis review in American Family Physician lists topical agents among options for the palms and soles, alongside iontophoresis and systemic agents [12]. Dermatology reviews also note that instruction on proper method and timing of antiperspirant use enhances its effect [2].

Dermatology reviews say aluminium salts work through a chemical reaction that forms plugs in the eccrine sweat ducts [2]. Other descriptions add that the salts interact with keratin fibrils in the duct and that the plug is lost as the outer skin layer sheds, so the effect wears off and applications are repeated [3]. The size of the sweat reduction varies between individuals [3].

The hexahydrate is an acidic salt, which is related to the stinging some users describe; the anhydrous industrial form is corrosive on handling [4]. A 1941 patent by Jules Montenier combined aluminium chloride with a soluble nitrile to reduce acidity and irritation, an early step in making aluminium-based antiperspirants wearable [3].

Irritation is the commonly reported effect of prescription-strength products. Users in forums describe burning or stinging and discuss remedies such as talcum powder [11]. Aluminium was named Allergen of the Year for 2022 by the American Contact Dermatitis Society, reflecting recognition of aluminium contact allergy, which is uncommon [13].

Public concern has centred on breast cancer and Alzheimer's disease. The US National Cancer Institute states that there is no scientific evidence linking antiperspirants to breast cancer while noting that studies have given conflicting results [3]. A 2005 review examined the question of aluminium in antiperspirants and breast cancer [10], and a 2014 systematic review of 469 studies found little evidence that aluminium exposure raises Alzheimer's, genetic damage or cancer risk [3]. In the US the FDA has noted that people with kidney disease are advised to consult a doctor before using aluminium-containing antiperspirants [3]. Animal studies have examined aluminium chloride toxicity at exposures unrelated to skin use [14].

Commercial antiperspirants date to the early twentieth century, with Everdry sold in 1903 and Stopette, which used Montenier's 1941 aluminium chloride formulation, following [3]. In the United States, deodorant-antiperspirant combinations are regulated as drugs, and the FDA's 2003 review of aluminium-containing antiperspirants left their status unchanged [3]. The EU Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety assessed aluminium compounds in consumer antiperspirants in a 2020 opinion and gave maximum concentrations it considered safe for cosmetic products [3].

An early open trial in 1978 evaluated 25 percent aluminium chloride hexahydrate in absolute ethanol for underarm hyperhidrosis [9]. A 1990 single-blind, half-sided study of 12 patients applied 20 percent aluminium chloride in ethanol to one palm daily for four weeks and measured water loss with an evaporimeter; treated palms showed a significant fall in skin water vapour loss compared with untreated palms [7].

A randomised clinical trial published in 2023 compared aluminium chloride hexahydrate gel iontophoresis with tap water iontophoresis in primary palmar hyperhidrosis [15], and a 2025 randomised comparison examined aluminium chloride, oxybutynin and botulinum toxin in primary focal hyperhidrosis [8]. Another trial from 1990 tested aluminium chloride on blistering in epidermolysis bullosa simplex [16].

Registered studies include one comparing non-prescription with prescription topical treatments and no treatment for sweating in 24 participants [17], a phase 3 comparison of topical aluminium chloride with botulinum toxin injections in residual-limb hyperhidrosis [18], and a small study of antiperspirant in prosthesis users [19]. A 2026 review of newer hyperhidrosis options lists aluminium chloride hexahydrate among conventional treatments alongside glycopyrronium bromide, sofpironium bromide and other newer approaches [20].
